No: gating only residual updates preserves a computational shortcut, not guaranteed influence from distant inputs. For h⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ₜ = h⁽ˡ⁾ₜ + g⁽ˡ⁾ₜ ⊙ Fₗ(h⁽ˡ⁾)ₜ, closing the gate retains whatever history preceding blocks already encoded at position t. The identity shortcut itself does not move information across time. If earlier gates prevent historical mixing, distant inputs may never reach t; learned transformations or the readout can also suppress or cancel their contribution. This architectural deduction distinguishes possible dependency from effective influence, consistent with research on [effective receptive fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.04128).

A strict raw-input window W requires output invariance to every input before t−W+1. Local operations on hidden states do not establish that bound: those states can already contain older history. For stride-one causal convolutions with kernel widths kₗ and dilations dₗ, the maximum receptive-field span is R = 1 + Σₗ(kₗ−1)dₗ, counting every convolution inside residual blocks; reachable positions can have gaps. Gates with broader dependencies can enlarge this span. Enforcing a strict window requires restricting every computational path, including gate inputs and inherited hidden states. [NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) explicitly uses dilated convolutions and residual blocks to expand historical reach.

Novelty should therefore be calibrated narrowly: [WaveNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.03499) already combines gated activations with dilated causal residual convolutions, while [ReZero](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04887) directly scales residual updates using learned gates. Adding a residual gate is straightforward; demonstrating useful adaptive historical influence requires controlled ablations and input-perturbation measurements. Neither guaranteed distant-history retention nor a strict sliding-window bound follows from gating residual updates alone.
